tips.title: And multiplies, or adds
tips.body: One choice **and** then another multiplies the ways. A choice **between** two things adds them. Reading which the question means decides everything that follows.

tips.title: Ask how many are left
tips.body: At each position, ask what is still available. With repeats allowed the number stays the same; without repeats it falls by one each time, giving $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7$ rather than $10^4$.

tips.title: Does order matter?
tips.body: A code, a queue or a finishing order: order **matters**. A team, a committee or a set of toppings: it does **not**, so divide by the number of ways the chosen items could be ordered.

tips.title: Write the boxes before the numbers
tips.body: Draw one box per position first, then fill each with how many choices remain. The boxes make repeats visible: with no repeats allowed the numbers fall 10, 9, 8, 7 instead of staying at 10, and the drop is obvious on the page rather than remembered.

why.matters:
The counting principle is one line — if this can happen $m$ ways and then that can happen $n$ ways, together they can happen $mn$ ways — and it is one line that does an enormous amount of work.

What makes it worth understanding rather than memorising is **how fast multiplying runs away from you**. Adding a single choice does not add to the total, it multiplies it. Nothing about everyday experience prepares you for how quickly that gets large, which is exactly why it is useful.

examples.title: Why a longer password beats a clever one
examples.body:
A 4-digit PIN has 10 choices in each position, so there are $10^4 = 10,000$ of them. A computer tries all of those in under a second, which is why a phone limits your attempts rather than relying on the number.

Now letters. 4 lowercase letters give $26^4 = 456,976$ — better, still nothing. But 6 letters give 308,915,776, and 8 give 208,827,064,576.

Look at what those two extra letters did: they multiplied the work by $26^2 = 676$, every time. That is the whole argument for length over cleverness. Substituting 3 for an e multiplies your 676s by almost nothing; adding two more characters multiplies them by 676 again.

visual.alt: A table of password lengths against the number of possible passwords, growing from ten thousand for a four digit PIN to over two hundred billion for eight lowercase letters

steps.title: The product rule for counting
steps.body:
When you make **one choice after another**, the number of ways multiply.

Edexcel states it like this: if there are $m$ ways of doing one task and, for each of those, $n$ ways of doing another, then the two together can be done in $m \times n$ ways.

It keeps going for more choices. Three tops and two pairs of trousers give $3 \times 2 = 6$ outfits. Add two pairs of shoes and it becomes $3 \times 2 \times 2 = 12$.

The words to watch for are **and** and **then**. *A starter **and** a main* multiplies. *A starter **or** a main* does not, because that is a choice between them, and you add instead.

visuals.alt: Four boxes about the product rule for counting: what it says, the word that signals it, an example and the warning about or
A table listing all six outfits from three tops and two bottoms, showing that the list matches three times two

check.prompt: A cafe offers 4 sandwiches and 3 drinks. How many different sandwich and drink combinations are there?
check.solution: One choice then another, so multiply: $4 \times 3 = 12$.

steps.title: Three courses, and why listing agrees
steps.body:
A menu offers **2 starters**, **3 mains** and **2 puddings**. How many three-course meals are possible?

The product rule answers it in one line. Listing shows **why** the answer is right, which is what a *show that* question wants.

steps.text: Choose a starter: **2** ways
For each of those, choose a main: **3** ways
For each of **those**, choose a pudding: **2** ways
$2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12$ meals
steps.note: one line, once you trust the rule

steps.text: Listing them systematically also gives 12, which is the check
steps.note: the list and the product must agree

visuals.alt: A table showing the start and end of a systematic list of the twelve three-course meals

check.prompt: A shop sells 5 phone cases and 4 screen protectors. How many ways are there to buy one of each?

steps.title: When the number of choices changes
steps.body:
The product rule still works when each choice has a **different** number of options, and that is where most marks are won or lost.

A four-digit code using digits 0 to 9, where digits **may repeat**, has $10,000$ possibilities: $10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10$, because every position still has all ten digits available.

If **no digit may repeat**, the count falls at each step: $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 5,040$. Ten choices for the first, but only nine left for the second, and so on.

So the question to ask before multiplying is always: **how many are left for this position?**

props.title: One word changes the answer by half

visuals.alt: A table comparing four digit codes with and without repeated digits, showing the number of choices at each position

steps.text: The first digit can be any of **10**
The second can be any of the **9** left
The third has **8** left, and the fourth **7**
$10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 5,040$
steps.note: multiply what is available at each step

check.prompt: How many three-digit codes can be made from the digits 0 to 9 if no digit may be repeated?
check.solution: $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$. The pool of digits shrinks by one at each position.

steps.title: Arrangements
steps.body:
**Arranging** things in order is the product rule with a shrinking pool. Arranging all of them has a shortcut: multiply every whole number down to 1.

The letters of **MATHS** are all different, so there are $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$ arrangements. That product is written $5!$ and read *five factorial*.

visuals.problem: Count the arrangements of the letters of MATHS

steps.text: The first letter can be any of **5**
The second can be any of the **4** left
Then **3**, then **2**, then **1**
steps.note: the last position has no choice left

steps.text: $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$
The final 1 is worth writing. Forgetting the shrinking pool gives $5^5$, which is far too big

visuals.alt: A table of factorials from one to six, showing how quickly the number of arrangements grows

check.prompt: In how many different orders can 4 people stand in a line?

steps.title: Restrictions: deal with them first
steps.body:
A question that restricts one position is the standard Higher tier version. The rule is simple: **fill the restricted position first**, then count what is left for the others.

Here are three-digit numbers made from the digits **1, 2, 3, 4, 5**, with no digit repeated.

steps.text: 'Even' restricts the **last** digit, so start there
steps.note: never start at the left when there is a restriction

steps.text: The last digit must be 2 or 4: **2** choices
The first digit is then any of the **4** remaining
steps.note: one digit has been used at the end

steps.text: The middle digit is any of the **3** left
$2 \times 4 \times 3 = 24$
steps.note: and enumerating all of them gives the same

steps.text: Out of $60$ altogether, so $P(\text{even}) = \dfrac{24}{60} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

visuals.alt: A table showing the number of choices at each position for three digit numbers from one to five with no repeats, under three different restrictions

check.prompt: Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 with no repeats, how many three-digit numbers are 300 or more?
check.solution: The first digit must be 3, 4 or 5, so **3** choices. Then 4 remain for the second and 3 for the third: $3 \times 4 \times 3 = 36$.

steps.title: Your turn: count, then check by listing
steps.body:
A lock code is **one letter followed by two digits**. Letters are A to Z and digits are 0 to 9, and repeats are allowed.

1. How many codes are possible?
2. How many end in an even digit?
3. How many use no digit twice?

Then try a small case you can list in full: how many two-letter codes are there using only A, B and C with no letter repeated? List them and check against your product.

check.prompt: A code is one letter from A to Z followed by two digits from 0 to 9, repeats allowed. How many codes are possible?

steps.title: Going deeper: does the order matter?
steps.body:
The question that separates top answers is whether **order matters**.

*In how many orders can five runners finish?* Order matters: first and second are different outcomes, so it is $5! = 120$.

*How many ways can two of five people be chosen for a team?* Order does **not** matter: choosing Amy and Ben is the same team as Ben and Amy. Counting arrangements would give $5 \times 4 = 20$, but every team has been counted **twice**, once in each order, so the answer is $20 \div 2 = 10$.

So when order does not matter, count the arrangements and then **divide by the number of ways the chosen items could be ordered**. For two chosen that is 2, for three chosen it is $3! = 6$.

Counting also feeds straight into probability. Once you know how many outcomes there are altogether and how many are wanted, the probability is the one over the other, provided the outcomes are equally likely.

rows: Two people chosen from five for a team
Three pizza toppings chosen from six

visuals.problem: How many ways can 3 pizza toppings be chosen from 6?

steps.text: If order mattered: $6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$
steps.note: three choices from a shrinking pool

steps.text: But cheese, ham, olives is the **same pizza** as olives, ham, cheese
Each set of 3 has been counted $3! = 6$ times, once per ordering
$120 \div 6 = \mathbf{20}$
Saying *why* you divided is where the mark is

check.prompt: Why is choosing 2 people from 5 for a team not simply 5 × 4?
check.solution: $5 \times 4$ counts **arrangements**, so Amy then Ben and Ben then Amy are counted separately. The same team twice, so divide by 2.
options: There are only 4 people left after the first
Each pair would be counted twice, once in each order
The two people must be different
The team could also have 3 members

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The **product rule**: $m$ ways then $n$ ways gives $m \times n$ altogether. **And** or **then** means multiply.
- **Or** means a choice between, so you **add** rather than multiply.
- Ask at each position: **how many are left?** With repeats allowed the number stays the same; without repeats it falls by one each time.
- Four-digit codes: $10,000$ with repeats, $5,040$ without.
- **Arranging** all of $n$ different items gives $n!$, meaning $n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 1$. Five items give $120$.
- With a **restriction**, fill the restricted position **first**, then count what remains.
- If **order does not matter**, count the arrangements and divide by the number of orderings of the chosen items.
- A **systematic list** proves the count is right, and is what a *show that* question wants.
- Counting feeds probability: wanted outcomes over total outcomes, when all are equally likely.

rows: m ways then n ways gives m × n
add: it is a choice between
the same number of choices each time
divide by the orderings of what was chosen

questions.prompt: A menu has 3 starters and 5 mains. How many two-course meals are possible?
questions.solution: One choice then another, so multiply: $3 \times 5 = 15$.

questions.prompt: A shop sells T-shirts in 4 colours and 3 sizes. How many different T-shirts are there?
Which word in a question tells you to multiply the number of choices?
questions.solution: **And** joins one choice to another, so the ways multiply. **Or** means a choice between, so you add.

questions.prompt: In how many different orders can 3 books be put on a shelf?
How many four-digit codes can be made from the digits 0 to 9 if digits may be repeated?
questions.solution: Every position still has all ten digits: $10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10,000$.

questions.prompt: How many four-digit codes can be made from the digits 0 to 9 if no digit may be repeated?
In how many different orders can 5 people stand in a queue?
A code has 3 positions, each a digit 0 to 9 with repeats allowed. Why is the answer not 10 × 9 × 8?
questions.solution: The pool only shrinks when repeats are **banned**. With repeats allowed every position has all ten digits, giving $10^3 = 1000$.
options: There are only 9 digits from 0 to 9
The first digit cannot be zero
Repeats are allowed, so all ten digits stay available
The order of the digits does not matter

questions.prompt: A restaurant offers 6 mains and 4 puddings. A meal is one main and one pudding. How many meals are possible?
Why is a systematic list useful even when the product rule gives the answer in one line?
questions.solution: The list **proves** the answer. A *show that* question wants the reasoning, and an order you can defend shows nothing has been missed.
options: It shows the count is right and nothing is missing
It avoids having to know the product rule
It works when the outcomes are not equally likely

questions.prompt: Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 with no digit repeated, how many three-digit numbers can be made?
Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 with no digit repeated, how many three-digit numbers are even?
questions.solution: Fill the restricted position first. The last digit must be 2 or 4, so 2 choices, then 4 remain and then 3: $2 \times 4 \times 3 = 24$.

questions.prompt: A code is one letter from A to Z followed by two digits from 0 to 9, with repeats allowed. How many such codes are there?
How many ways can 2 people be chosen from 5 for a team, when the order they are chosen in does not matter?
questions.solution: Arranging two from five gives $5 \times 4 = 20$, but each pair is counted twice, once in each order. So $20 \div 2 = 10$.

markScheme.description: divides by 2 because order does not matter

questions.prompt: How many ways can 3 toppings be chosen from 6, when the order does not matter?
questions.solution: Arranging three from six gives $6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$. Each set of three is counted $3! = 6$ times, so $120 \div 6 = 20$.

questions.prompt: A four-digit PIN is chosen at random with no digit repeated. Which calculation gives the probability of guessing it first time?
questions.solution: There are $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 5040$ equally likely codes and exactly one is right, so the probability is $\dfrac{1}{5040}$.

questions.prompt: Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, with no digit repeated, work out how many three-digit numbers are even. Explain your method.
questions.solution: The restriction is on the last digit, so that position is filled first. For the number to be even the last digit must be 2 or 4, which gives two choices. Once that digit has been used, four digits remain for the first position, and once two have been used, three remain for the middle. Multiplying gives two times four times three, which is twenty four. Filling the restricted position first matters, because starting at the left would leave the number of even digits still available depending on what had already been chosen.

markScheme.description: identifies the last digit as the restricted position
4 and 3 choices for the remaining positions

criteria.text: Identifies that the restriction is on the last digit and fills it first
States there are 2 choices for the last digit, namely 2 and 4
States 4 choices then 3 for the remaining two positions

questions.modelAnswer:
**Fill the restricted position first.** For the number to be **even**, the last digit must be **2 or 4**: two choices.

**Then the rest.** One digit has been used, so the first position has **4** left. Two are now used, so the middle has **3** left.

$$2 \times 4 \times 3 = \mathbf{24}$$

**Why fill the last position first?** Starting at the left would leave the number of even digits still available depending on which digit had already been chosen, so the count would not be a single multiplication.

questions.prompt: A team of 2 is chosen from 5 people. A student says the answer is 5 × 4 = 20. Explain what is wrong and give the correct answer.
questions.solution: Five times four counts the number of ways of choosing two people in order, treating the first chosen and the second chosen as different roles. For a team the order does not matter, so choosing Amy then Ben gives the same team as choosing Ben then Amy. Every team has therefore been counted twice, once in each order. Dividing twenty by two gives ten, which is the number of different teams.

markScheme.description: states that each team is counted twice

criteria.text: Explains that 5 × 4 counts the choices in order
States that each team has been counted twice, once in each order

questions.modelAnswer:
**What 5 × 4 counts.** It counts the ways of choosing two people **in order**, as if being picked first were different from being picked second.

**Why that is wrong here.** For a **team**, order does not matter: choosing Amy then Ben gives the **same team** as choosing Ben then Amy. So every team has been counted **twice**, once in each order.

$$20 \div 2 = \mathbf{10}$$

examTechnique.body:
Before multiplying anything, ask two questions about each position in turn: how many options does it have, and does using one remove it from the next? That second question is the whole difference between $10^4$ and $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7$.

When the question restricts a position, fill **that** position first and count outwards from it. Starting at the left and meeting the restriction at the end forces you to split into cases, which is where arithmetic goes wrong.

Watch **and** against **or**. And multiplies, or adds.

Ask whether order matters. If the answer is a code, a queue or a finishing order, it does. If it is a team, a committee or a set of toppings, it does not, and you divide by the orderings of whatever was chosen.

On a *show that* question, list systematically. The list is the reasoning, and the reasoning is the marks.
examinerErrors: Using the same number of choices at every position when repeats are banned, so 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 instead of 10 × 9 × 8 × 7.
Adding when the question says and, or multiplying when it says or.
Starting at the left when a restriction applies to the last position.
Forgetting the final × 1 when writing out a factorial, which does no harm, or writing n to the power n instead, which does.
Counting a team as though order mattered, so every selection is counted twice.
Dividing by 2 when three items were chosen, where the correction is 3! = 6.
Listing outcomes at random rather than systematically, then missing one.
Giving the number of outcomes when the question asked for a probability.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes down the number of choices at each position before multiplying, and says whether repeats are allowed. Faced with a restriction it fills that position first and explains why. It decides out loud whether order matters, and when it does not, divides by the number of orderings of the chosen items rather than always by two. It can turn a count into a probability, checking first that the outcomes are equally likely, and on a show that question it lists systematically rather than asserting the product.
